paras: The threatened lynching of Joe Ebright took place at Las Vegas, New Mexico, in March 1881, after Ebright, a saloon keeper, shot and killed James H. Curry, a freight conductor on the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe railroad, and railroad men talked of hanging him. The sheriff swore in special deputies and fortified the jail, and a justice of the peace discharged Ebright three days later when no one appeared to prosecute. It drew national notice because a Philadelphia dispatch misidentified the dead man as James Currie, the killer of the actor Benjamin Porter.

Curry was a freight conductor popular among the railroad men based at Las Vegas, and Ebright, by his own account thirty-five and born in Ohio, had come from Denver with his wife, "the woman Bertha," who kept the house where the shooting took place.

Ebright shot Curry on the forenoon of Wednesday, March 23, 1881. Ebright told the Gazette that Curry, quarreling over a torn five-dollar bill, threatened to kill him with a cocked six-shooter, and that he crawled behind the counter to his own pistol, then sprang up and fired. Others said Curry was sober, had been shot in the back of the head, and that the pistol beside him was not his.

A Denver dispatch reported "the general impression" that the shooting was uncalled for and that threats of lynching "were freely indulged in." Excitement among railroad men grew as evening came, and the Gazette wrote that Ebright would have been hanged before night if only a small force had guarded the jail. Instead Sheriff Romero swore in a large posse of special deputies and carried guns into the jail, and the talk of lynching was dropped.
That night east-side citizens formed a committee to assist the police, which the Gazette insisted was "in no sense a vigilance committee."
A warrant charging Ebright with murder was sworn out before Judge Steele, and he was held in jail awaiting a preliminary examination.

On March 26 Ebright appeared before Justice of the Peace Jose Montoya, and when no prosecution was offered he was discharged. He was rearrested for breach of the peace, discharged again by Justice Steel, and that night a number of men were said to be hunting for him without success. A Montana paper later reported that he "escaped from the city before a mob could hang him."

Most papers outside New Mexico printed a Philadelphia dispatch of March 30, from a private message to U.S. Marshal Kerns, which named the dead man as "James Currie, the murderer of Porter, the actor," and dated the killing March 24. It said Currie had been on a drunken spree, that railroad hands "attempted to lynch the bartender," and that a coroner's jury found self-defense. It ran from Washington, Richmond and Dallas to Wheeling, Arizona and Dakota, and the New York Evening Post saw "special Providence" in its parallels with the Porter killing.

Headlines treated the killing as justice for Porter: "Righteous Retribution," "A Good Ridance," "Porter's Murderer Gone to His Account" and "Met His Fate at Last," while the Wheeling Register headed it "A Narrow Escape from Lynching."

Corrections followed: a Leavenworth dispatch in the Chicago Tribune of March 31 said the dead man was a Santa Fe freight conductor, and a Little Rock dispatch called him a former Memphis and Little Rock conductor. The Gazette told the Tribune's S. J. Medill that the Porter story was not correct, and it later mocked a Police Gazette picture headed "Jim Currie's Fate."
The Las Vegas paper called the killing a "dastardly" murder and praised the sheriff for saving bloodshed. None of the reports gave the race of Curry, Ebright or the railroad men.
The date differs: the Gazette's March 24 issue placed the shooting "yesterday forenoon," the Philadelphia dispatch gave March 24, and an Ohio weekly gave "the 30th ult."

The wire said railroad hands attempted to lynch the bartender, while the Gazette reported lynching talk that was dropped once the jail was guarded. Wire reports said a coroner's jury found self-defense, but the Gazette reported a murder warrant and a discharge for want of prosecution.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Railroad men threatened to hang saloon keeper Joe Ebright, held in jail for killing conductor James H. Curry, until the sheriff fortified the jail (A2, A1, A22); the wire called it an attempted lynching (A7).
Railroad men talked of hanging Ebright for the killing of Curry and later hunted him (A2, A5, A35), but no one was killed by a mob; Ebright escaped (A35).

The local Gazette (A2) and the separate Denver (A1, A22) and Philadelphia (A7) dispatches agree that a shooting by a saloon keeper was followed by lynch threats from railroad men and protection by the sheriff, though they differ on details.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Philadelphia wire under headlines such as 'Righteous Retribution' and 'A Good Ridance', treating the death as deserved.
The Las Vegas Gazette condemned Ebright's 'dastardly' act but praised the sheriff for preventing a lynching and stressed its committee was not a vigilance committee.
The Knoxville Chronicle, quoting the New York Evening Post, read the case as 'special Providence'.
